newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss seek to accelerate Nazi Germany probe.
newsitem.headline: Swiss seek to accelerate Nazi Germany probe.

text.p: The Swiss government, trying to speed up investigations into the country's dealings with Nazi Germany, has asked parliament to suspend a three-month waiting period for voters to object to new laws, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Thursday.
Switzerland's strict laws on banking secrecy could therefore be eased as early as December or January 1, 1997, instead of April, 1997, he said.
The upper house of parliament is due to vote in December on a decree that would create a commission of experts empowered to lift banking secrecy laws.
This would enable the experts to fully investigate Swiss financial dealings with Nazi Germany and the fate of Jewish wealth deposited before, during and after World War Two.
"The government wants an urgent decision," the spokesman said, noting that this meant parliament would have to approve a suspension of the normal three-month period for voters to object to a law.
Any law passed by Switzerland's parliament can be put to a full referendum if 50,000 signatures are gathered.

The lower house of parliament voted on September 30 to create a commission of experts to write an historical account of Swiss commerce with Nazi Germany, which used Swiss gold purchases to help to finance its war effort.

The commission will also try to calculate how much wealth was deposited in Switzerland by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution and judge whether the Swiss had done enough to identify the lost assets of those killed in the Holocaust.

The Swiss Foreign Ministry has also formed two new expert panels to probe mounting accusations that the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims from Eastern Europe was used to compensate Swiss citizens for nationalised property.

Switzerland faces suspicions, fuelled by newly-declassified U.S. wartime archives, that it could still be hoarding Nazi gold or holding millions of dollars in assets from people who perished during the war.
The country has struggled to deal with sharp criticism from Jewish groups and influential U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato about the way it handled dormant accounts from Holocaust victims.

A banking ombudsman is coordinating nearly 1,000 claims that have been submitted so far and an independent panel set up by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers will also comb bank records for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous sweeps.
